name: valence_salience_listener
detail: ELPD-LOO -17429.1
hypothesis: Listeners interpret referential statements by modeling a speaker whose object choices reflect their evaluative attitude: under positive framing ("favorite"), speakers favor feature-rich objects, whereas under negative framing ("least favorite"), they disfavor them. Listeners invert this evaluative preference alongside literal semantics to infer the intended referent, and rely on it directly when no informative word is spoken.

name: base_rate_tracking_listener
detail: ELPD-LOO -17433.9
hypothesis: Listeners integrate pragmatic speaker reasoning with empirical base rates established during prior familiarization, weighting referents by their baseline exposure frequency rather than assuming an equiprobable prior over objects. On conflict displays such as the low-baserate target condition of experiment E5, where a rare implicature target (base rate 1/9) competes with a highly familiar two-feature object (base rate 7/9), depth-2 RSA predicts near-exclusive choice of the implicature target (>94%) because it assumes uniform priors, whereas base-rate tracking predicts that the familiar competitor will be chosen frequently (~40%), matching human choices.

name: costly_feature_speaker
detail: ELPD-LOO -17428.2
hypothesis: Speakers incur an explicit communicative cost when producing ambiguous words that apply to multiple objects in the scene, preferring unique descriptors even beyond what literal informativeness dictates. Listeners reason about this ambiguity-averse speaker, inferring that a speaker who chose a shared word must have lacked any less ambiguous alternative for their intended referent.

name: feature_prior_l2
detail: ELPD-LOO -17416.9
hypothesis: Listeners maintain an inductive prior over objects based on their feature count rather than assuming all referents are equally likely, favoring simpler objects with fewer features as default referents. This improves fit because participants exhibit a systematic preference for less modified objects when choosing referents and when encountering uninformative utterances, which uniform-prior depth-2 reasoning fails to capture. Differences from rsa_l2: - Recursion depth: unchanged (choice_probs calls L2, depth 2). - Parameters added: feature_weight (Normal(0.0, 1.0)). - Parameters removed: none. - Other terms: choice_probs computes an object prior from feature counts via softmax_prior(feature_weight * ctx.feature_count); L1 and L2 pass this prior to the speaker (wpp=vec(prior, r) instead of wpp=1); and choice_probs uses this prior rather than a uniform distribution on uninformative prior trials (ctx.is_prior > 0).

name: base_rate_prior_l2
detail: ELPD-LOO -17437.4
hypothesis: Listeners reason at depth 2 while integrating familiarization base rates into their prior expectations about which referent the speaker intends to convey, choosing by base rate when no informative word is spoken. Compared to rsa_l2, this refines the object prior from uniform to familiarization base rates (defaulting to uniform when absent), explaining human sensitivity to exposure frequency in reference games. Differences from rsa_l2: recursion depth is unchanged (choice_probs calls L2); no parameters are added or removed (retaining alpha and lapse); L0, L1, and L2 take an object prior vector derived from familiarization base rates, and choice_probs returns this prior on uninformative prior trials.

name: feature_simplicity_listener
detail: ELPD-LOO -17413.4
hypothesis: We refine rsa_l1 by introducing a feature-simplicity prior over referents, positing that communicators expect referents with fewer defining features to be targeted more readily than complex referents. In choice_probs, recursion depth remains unchanged at depth 1 (calling L1), one parameter is added (simplicity with a Normal(0, 1) prior), and no parameters are removed. In L1, the speaker samples referents according to a softmax prior over object feature counts rather than uniformly, and uninformative prior trials predict this prior rather than a uniform distribution.

name: feature_distinctiveness_listener
detail: ELPD-LOO -17418.9
hypothesis: Listeners maintain an inductive prior over referents grounded in contextual feature distinctiveness, expecting communicators to target objects whose features are rare or unique within the display rather than shared across many items. Rather than evaluating features in isolation or assuming an equiprobable prior over referents, listeners weight candidate referents by their contextual distinctiveness relative to the surrounding scene. When interpreting an utterance or choosing in the absence of an informative message, listeners integrate this contextual distinctiveness prior with pragmatic speaker reasoning.

name: selective_attention_listener
detail: ELPD-LOO -17413.5
hypothesis: Listeners have limited visual attention across the display, selectively focusing on candidate referents compatible with the heard utterance while discounting unattended distractors in the visual background. When evaluating the speaker's communicative alternatives, the listener computes informativeness primarily over the attended candidates, so non-matching distractors exert attenuated influence on pragmatic inference. In the absence of an informative utterance, the listener allocates attention uniformly across the available objects.

name: graded_truth_listener
detail: ELPD-LOO -17424.0
hypothesis: Word meanings possess graded truth values rather than binary all-or-nothing applicability: a word is a more prototypical and semantically fitting descriptor for an object that minimally exemplifies the feature than for an object cluttered with extraneous features. Communicators reason over these graded truth values, so that listeners treat simpler referents as more semantically compatible with the utterance and infer that speakers describing multi-feature objects face diminished semantic fit.

name: costly_simplicity_listener

name: referential_prominence_listener
detail: ELPD-LOO -17415.1

name: fewest_features_listener

name: softmax_decision_listener

Listeners interpret utterances by jointly reasoning about the speaker's communicative goal and intended referent, inferring that mentioning a shared feature implies the speaker lacked any more distinctive aspect to convey. In the absence of an informative message, listeners choose uniformly among the available objects.

name: base_rate_tracking_listener
detail: elpd_diff 42.1 > 2.0 x clustered dse 16.8 vs conservative_base_rate_simplicity (grouped CV)
hypothesis: Listeners integrate pragmatic speaker reasoning with empirical base rates established during prior familiarization, weighting referents by their baseline exposure frequency rather than assuming an equiprobable prior over objects. On conflict displays such as the low-baserate target condition of experiment E5, where a rare implicature target (base rate 1/9) competes with a highly familiar two-feature object (base rate 7/9), depth-2 RSA predicts near-exclusive choice of the implicature target (>94%) because it assumes uniform priors, whereas base-rate tracking predicts that the familiar competitor will be chosen frequently (~40%), matching human choices.

name: base_rate_prior_l2
detail: elpd_diff 45.9 > 2.0 x clustered dse 21.1 vs conservative_base_rate_simplicity (grouped CV)
hypothesis: Listeners reason at depth 2 while integrating familiarization base rates into their prior expectations about which referent the speaker intends to convey, choosing by base rate when no informative word is spoken. Compared to rsa_l2, this refines the object prior from uniform to familiarization base rates (defaulting to uniform when absent), explaining human sensitivity to exposure frequency in reference games. Differences from rsa_l2: recursion depth is unchanged (choice_probs calls L2); no parameters are added or removed (retaining alpha and lapse); L0, L1, and L2 take an object prior vector derived from familiarization base rates, and choice_probs returns this prior on uninformative prior trials.

name: fewest_features_listener
detail: elpd_diff 308.6 > 2.0 x clustered dse 55.0 vs conservative_base_rate_simplicity (grouped CV)
hypothesis: Listeners do not reason counterfactually about an informative speaker; instead, they follow a direct simplicity heuristic that favors objects with fewer features. When hearing a word, listeners filter the visual display to objects literally matching that word and select among them with a bias toward objects with fewer total features. In the absence of an informative utterance, listeners rely directly on this simplicity preference across all available objects.

name: literal_listener
detail: elpd_diff 1208.6 > 2.0 x clustered dse 209.5 vs conservative_base_rate_simplicity (grouped CV)
hypothesis: Listeners pick uniformly among the objects the word is literally true of.
